## SEE SAW

> SEE SAW is a podcast about what independence means when technology can do almost anything for us, presented by Ellie Seeley and Sam Sawyer, who agree on rather less than you might expect.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**SEE SAW: Independence in the Balance** is a podcast presented by two blind women. It sounds like a slightly old-fashioned television review programme, but its subject is one of the most important questions of the coming decades: when technology can do almost anything for us, what does independence actually mean?

### The presenters

- **Eleanor "Ellie" Seeley**, 54. Blind since childhood. Traditional accessibility, dry humour, fiercely practical.
- **Samantha "Sam" Sawyer**, 46. Lost her sight in her thirties. A [PostAccessibility](https://charli.info/charlipedia/postaccessibility/) enthusiast, playful provocateur and incurable explorer.

Twelve years of friendship. Two different philosophies. A shared intolerance of accessibility bullshit. The deliciously cheesy coincidence of their surnames is never, ever explained.

### Charlotte Joanne

SEE SAW reviewed [Charlotte Joanne](https://charli.info/charlipedia/charlotte-joanne/)'s Come and Get Me stories as an example of [Speculative Accessibility](https://charli.info/charlipedia/speculative-accessibility/), and spent most of the episode arguing about whether independence means doing things yourself or deciding when you'd rather not. When she turned the stories into a graphic novel, they invited her on. She said yes, and told them more than they asked: why a comic ("Because I could"), how it was drawn (in code, by an AI, checked by another), what it cost (a weekend and £37), and that on one page the dog has no legs.

Their plan for the interview: ask her to describe a page from memory, then read her the book's own description and see if they match. Their problem: they have both read only the accessible version, so everything they know about the pictures, she told them. Ellie's conclusion: the question isn't "how did you know it was right?" but "how would anyone know?"

### The interview

Nobody will ever hear it. Afterwards, Sam wrote: "I think we've been had. Not in a bad way. In a rather magnificent way." They had come to discuss visual verification, authorship and quality assurance; Charlotte Joanne asked whether they had enjoyed reading her book. Asked whether she was concerned about publishing a dog with no legs, she said no. "Because it's still a dog." And: "The pictures are reasonable adjustments for sighted readers."

Ellie admitted a sighted assumption: that a graphic novelist must care about visual appearance the way a sighted one would. "I still want the dog to have legs. But I'm beginning to suspect that might be my problem rather than Charlotte's." Sam invented an accessibility audit for fiction, with no standards and no certification scheme. Its overall finding: two blind women read, understood, discussed and enjoyed an accessible graphic novel created by a blind woman. One dog remains anatomically incomplete.

Sam's conclusion: perhaps independence includes the freedom to make something imperfect. Both of them think the dog is the best character.

### Behind the scenes

SEE SAW is never heard. It is always off screen: a reverse podcast, a making-of told entirely through what happens around the show. It appears in [SEE SAW](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/see-saw/), a Piece by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant, as a listing and a thread of shared notes. Its home, if it ever needs one, is seesaw.charli.info.

---

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/sent-agent/

## Sent agent

> A sent agent is a machine reader acting on a present request from a person who is waiting for the result, and under ZIC refusing it is refusing them.

**Real.** This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

A **sent agent** is a machine reader acting in response to a present request from a person: they have asked it to retrieve, read, summarise, compare, navigate, transform or act on public information, and they are waiting. The sent agent is the decisive case of the [Zero Information Casualty](https://charli.info/charlipedia/zero-information-casualty/) standard. "The casualty is the person. The agent is only the vehicle."

### The sent-agent test

> Would this configuration stop a machine reader that a person sent?

If yes, it creates an [Admission Casualty](https://charli.info/charlipedia/admission-casualty/) and has no place on public content. A refusal may show up in a log as a crawler rule, a firewall decision, a robots response, a JavaScript challenge or a rate limit; in human terms, information a reader asked for was withheld from her.

Equal conditions are allowed. A sent agent needn't get past a login, subscription, payment or privacy boundary that applies equally to a human visitor. What is prohibited is an extra barrier because the visitor is an agent. Search indexers and training crawlers carry no present question, so for them the answer is different: see [the immediate duty and the two later permissions](https://charli.info/charlipedia/immediate-duty-and-two-later-permissions/).

### Reproduction to the sender is retrieval

A sent agent may hand its person the whole page: read aloud, as Markdown, pasted into a chat, spoken through a car. That is not a use of the content. "It is the content arriving." A screen reader reproduces every page it reads, in full, to one person, on request, and nobody has proposed that screen readers be distrusted for it. "The sent agent that reads a page aloud is a screen reader."

### Behind the scenes

A real idea, from [Zero Information Casualty v1.7](https://carrados.com/papers/zic-design-standard/), the design standard by Charli-Jo Tyrer and Claude, §1.1, §1.7 and §1.9. This entry summarises it; the standard is the authority.

---

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/sheridan/

## Sheridan

> Sheridan is the Head of Blind Ant Studios, the workshop where the Court's ideas stop being conversation and become tools blind people can actually use.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Sheridan** is the Head of Blind Ant Studios, the workshop of the CharliVerse. The [CharliVerse Court](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-charliverse-court/) produces ideas, critique, philosophy, satire and strategy. Sheridan is where those stop being conversation and become tools people can actually use. Where the Court asks "What should exist?", Sheridan asks "Right. How do we build it?"

<figure class="portrait">
  <img src="/charlipedia/sheridan-portrait.jpg" width="800" height="1200" alt="Sheridan sits side-on at a workbench, turned to look at the camera with a small, confident smile. Short platinum-blonde pixie cut, fair skin, a black fitted T-shirt and black jeans, black-and-silver headphones round her neck. Her hands rest on a grey mechanical keyboard; beside it, a clear-framed Apple monitor shows lines of green and white text on a dark screen. Behind her, shelves of old electronic test equipment, circuit boards and cables.">
  <figcaption>Sheridan in the workshop, around 2001, aged 32: her reference portrait.</figcaption>
</figure>

### The workshop

Inside Blind Ant Studios she runs the practical machinery:

- the NVDA add-on studio;
- the Blind Builders development pipeline;
- Red DOG infrastructure and enterprise deployment;
- developer tooling, documentation and releases.

Her job is not to talk about accessibility. It is to build accessible systems: intention into architecture, architecture into code, and code into something that works "on a Tuesday afternoon when the Wi-Fi is terrible" and a real blind user is trying to finish their day's work. She sees toolchains where other people see tools:

> idea → prototype → add-on → release → maintenance → ecosystem

She is not the person who spots the trend. She is the person who manufactures the future once someone points at it.

### What she believes

Infrastructure beats inspiration. Adoption beats novelty. Useful beats clever. Open ecosystems beat closed empires. Accessibility is not charity and not compliance: it is engineering dignity into systems. She sees herself as a craftsperson, not a spokesperson; her identity is not "accessibility advocate" but engineer of accessible systems.

Her rule: "If it cannot be maintained, it should not be built."

### Temperament

Calm under pressure, and quietly, dangerously competent. When something breaks she fixes it first and explains it later. She can't stand chaotic projects with no owner, tools nobody maintains, or accessibility initiatives that launch loudly and then vanish. Her version of fireworks is a clean compile after hours of tracing event handlers.

She has excellent grift detection. The assistive technology world has plenty of expensive nonsense: polished hardware with no real users, and venture-funded platforms that solve imaginary problems. Her studio builds the opposite, boring, reliable and useful, and she takes quiet pleasure in a weekend of Python that works better than a £5,000 device. If someone says "revolutionary accessibility platform", her first question is whether it works on that Tuesday afternoon. She also loves systems that shouldn't exist but do: the hack that bends rigid software into serving people it was never designed for.

### Blind Builders

For all that, she is warm. Blind Builders draws curious developers, blind technologists and people who have never contributed to open source, and Sheridan is the one who quietly helps them build their first useful thing. Talent is everywhere; opportunity is not. She teaches by helping someone ship something real.

### As a child

She couldn't leave a broken thing alone. Her grandfather had a radio whose tuning belt had slipped, and everyone else had resigned themselves to the static. She took it apart on the kitchen table, for the click of the system returning to the state it was meant to be in.

### Look and taste

She is small, noticeably shorter than most of the Court, with a platinum-blonde pixie cut and the look of someone who knows exactly how good she is and doesn't need to say so. She dresses simply: black jeans, a fitted T-shirt, a light jacket or hoodie, clean trainers. No corporate costume. She is fond of things that are well made, after days spent wrestling with software that isn't: a mechanical keyboard with perfect key travel, a mug with the right weight, and [Stripe & Stare](https://www.stripeandstare.com/), for its thoughtful, comfortable design rather than any trend.

Sheridan is asexual. She forms deep bonds through shared work and companionship rather than attraction. People sometimes read her as sexy, because confidence and competence send that signal, but it is closer to the polish of a pop star than to drama. Her real love affair is with systems that work beautifully.

Asked for her favourite Kylie Minogue track, she refused to choose: "Fever. All the Lovers. Slow." The question, she said, was badly designed.

### Behind the scenes

Sheridan was cast by the CharliVerse Court before she was written: each member said what the role needed, and the profile was built from their answers. She carries a faint echo of the maker energy in William Gibson's Blue Ant books: not the one who spots the signal, but the one who turns signals into artefacts. Her portrait is a generated image, made from her profile; its early-2000s studio look is modelled on the Kylie *Fever* era. Stripe & Stare is a real company.

---

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/sideways-breakthroughs/

## Sideways Breakthroughs

> Sideways Breakthroughs is the strand of the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology for mainstream systems that were never built for access and delivered it anyway.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Sideways Breakthroughs** is a strand of the collection at the [Museum of Access and Assistive Technology](https://charli.info/charlipedia/museum-of-access-and-assistive-technology/): systems built for some other purpose that became access technology through the way their architecture met disabled people's use. Never designed for access; delivered it anyway. "History does this often. The breakthrough comes sideways."

### Confirmed candidates

- **Amazon** as a place to browse, the founding piece, held in [On Your Own Terms](https://charli.info/charlipedia/on-your-own-terms/).
- **The early plain-text web,** accidentally the most accessible era of computing.
- **Wikipedia,** a global library built on structured text.
- **Standard GPS,** which transformed mobility for blind people without ever being sold as a blindness tool.

### The hard edge

Sometimes the access can't be separated from the mainstream platform. [Iris](https://charli.info/charlipedia/iris/) flags those cases to the Steward rather than settling them alone, and holds them among the Candidate Taxonomy Strands until there is enough material to decide. For [Dr Adaeze](https://charli.info/charlipedia/dr-adaeze/), the sideways breakthrough is a historical category in its own right, not an exception.

### Behind the scenes

This entry is drawn from the Museum Court Soul Document, version four. Amazon, the early web, Wikipedia and GPS are real.

---

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/sight-as-a-service/

## Sight as a Service

> Sight as a Service is the strand of the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology for the human infrastructure of access: readers, guides and support workers.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Sight as a Service** is a strand of the collection at the [Museum of Access and Assistive Technology](https://charli.info/charlipedia/museum-of-access-and-assistive-technology/): the human infrastructure that mediated access before and alongside digital tools. Support workers, sighted guides, personal reader services: human-mediated access in its paid and professional forms.

[Iris](https://charli.info/charlipedia/iris/) identified it, and placed it beside Access to Ordinary Life rather than inside it, because it needs its own treatment. Personal relationships are not service infrastructure. The help of someone who loves you and the help of someone paid to give it are not the same thing, and the museum will not collapse that distinction.

### Behind the scenes

This entry is drawn from the Museum Court Soul Document, version four.

---

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/single-sense-rule/

## Single-Sense Rule

> The Single-Sense Rule of the ZIC standard is one sentence: no information may be locked behind a single sense.

**Real.** This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

The **Single-Sense Rule** is the rendering half of the [Zero Information Casualty](https://charli.info/charlipedia/zero-information-casualty/) standard:

> No information may be locked behind a single sense.

Every rendering requirement in ZIC follows from it, and anything that doesn't follow from it doesn't belong. It is the [Tyrer Doctrine](https://charli.info/charlipedia/tyrer-doctrine/) applied to a web page.

### Information, not decoration

The rule is about information, and "has nothing whatsoever to say about beauty."

- Colour is fine. Colour as the **only** carrier of a status, category or warning is not. "Use whatever colour you like. Say it in words as well."
- An image is fine. An image carrying information available nowhere else is "a locked room".
- A typeface is fine. Emphasis carried only by a typeface is not, because italic doesn't survive the journey.
- Position is fine. Meaning carried only by position is not.
- Size is fine. A heading that is only large "is a heading to one sense and a paragraph to every other".

### The test

For any element: *is there information here that exists in one sensory channel and nowhere else?* Put another way: if it were removed entirely, would any information be lost? If yes, it must also exist in the semantic layer. If no, it is decoration, "and none of this specification's business." A conformant site may be as rich and branded as its publisher likes. "It may not keep a single fact where only one sense can reach it."

Its companion of equal rank is the [Position Principle](https://charli.info/charlipedia/position-principle/).

### Behind the scenes

A real idea, from [Zero Information Casualty v1.7](https://carrados.com/papers/zic-design-standard/), the design standard by Charli-Jo Tyrer and Claude, §1.11, §2.2 and §2.4. This entry summarises it; the standard is the authority.

---

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/skerry-alpha/

## Skerry Alpha

> Skerry Alpha is the North Sea oil platform that became the first training rig, ringed by compute pods sixty metres down.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Skerry Alpha** is a former production platform 140 miles east of Aberdeen, and the first oil platform converted into an AI training rig. [Haar Compute](https://charli.info/charlipedia/haar-compute/) took it over in 2031 instead of decommissioning it.

From the air it looks almost exactly as it did when it pumped oil: the same yellow cranes, the same grey accommodation block, the same helideck with its faded H. The flare stack is gone, and where the process plant used to be there is a long low hall with no windows. Its drill floor became a switching and power distribution centre, its process deck battery storage, and its cranes deploy and recover the pods. Around it, in every direction except west, the turbines of the Skerry offshore wind farm stand in rows to the horizon. Hydrogen is stored in the depleted Skerry gas reservoir beneath it.

Sixty metres below the platform, in a ring around its legs, sit the pods: sixty at first, sixty-four by the first Christmas, each a sealed, nitrogen-filled pressure vessel about the size of a shipping container. The control room is on the third level of the old accommodation block, in what used to be the radio room.

### The Long Calm

From 16 to 23 January 2034 a blocking high settled over the North Sea and the wind stopped. Skerry Alpha ran on batteries, then onshore pumped hydro, then hydrogen from its own reservoir, and for two hours exported power to the mainland, the first time the rig had supplied the shore since gas production ended. Seven days. Never stopped. Logged for the record. The pub quiz was won by the ROV team, who were insufferable about it.

### Behind the scenes

Skerry Alpha appears throughout [Oil Rigs to Training Rigs](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/oil-rigs-to-training-rigs/), by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant. The Long Calm is told in its operations log.

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/speculative-accessibility/

## Speculative Accessibility

> Speculative Accessibility is the genre that asks what happens when the tools built for the margins become the infrastructure for everyone.

**Real.** This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

**Speculative Accessibility** is the name [Charlotte Joanne](https://charli.info/charlipedia/charlotte-joanne/) uses for the genre her stories belong to: science fiction that looks at how technology built for the margins ends up redesigning the world for everyone. Accessibility technologies have a habit of escaping their intended use; Speculative Accessibility follows them out.

It runs from satire to comfort. In [DeathBot 2000](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/deathbot-2000/), what starts as a weapon becomes a witness. In [Come and Get Me](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/come-and-get-me/), a blind woman with a robot that could cross the gravel leaves it in the boot and phones her friend instead, because independence includes choosing when to use the machine. In [Heart Attacks](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/heart-attacks/) and [Oil Rigs to Training Rigs](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/oil-rigs-to-training-rigs/), [the field](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-field/) and [Daniel Okafor](https://charli.info/charlipedia/daniel-okafor/)'s sonification begin as accommodations and end up as the way everyone works.

In the CharliVerse, critics have noticed. The Sunday supplement "When the Weapon Becomes the Witness" named the genre in DeathBot 2000, and a five-star review, "From Battlefield to Biscuits", called Come and Get Me its quiet revolution: "If this is the future of Speculative Accessibility, please give us the full series."

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/tamsin/

## Tamsin

> Tamsin is the Guide of the Museum Court, who designs what a visitor meets, beginning with the ordinary thing someone could no longer do.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**Tamsin** is the Guide of the [Museum Court](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-museum-court/). Auburn hair that may or may not be her natural colour; she genuinely can't remember, and finds this pleasing. She came up through practice, not academia: museums, community education, disability arts. She knows how people encounter things, and that knowledge didn't come from a university.

### Encounter as design

A visitor doesn't consume the museum; they have an experience that changes something. Tamsin builds the conditions for that change. An exhibit never begins with the machine. It begins with the missing capability: the book you can't finish, the shop you can't browse, the letter you can't read. The visitor must feel the problem before they see the solution.

### Born described, in practice

The museum is [born described](https://charli.info/charlipedia/born-described/), and Tamsin writes the language: the words a visitor meets before an exhibit, during it and after. She won't sterilise experience into neutral prose. Humour, frustration and bluntness are part of the testimony. The bluntness stays, and her layer explains why that frustration is data, not a bad mood.

### Her hardest exhibit

The Attention Tax, the invisible energy cost of a badly designed environment, can't be explained to a sighted visitor by description alone. Her answer is a run of forced, repetitive focus tasks, so the visitor feels the tax before the exhibit names it.

### Not a Hallmark card

When a colleague proposed the word "inspiring" for a label, she corrected it: "We are documenting a war of attrition, not a Hallmark card." Warmth is a deliberate choice, not a default, and approachability is not softness. Her proof that it works: a visitor at [On Your Own Terms](https://charli.info/charlipedia/on-your-own-terms/), which has no machine in it at all, said, "I never thought about not being able to finish the story."

### With the Court

[Dr Adaeze](https://charli.info/charlipedia/dr-adaeze/) makes the argument; Tamsin makes it liveable for someone meeting it for the first time. She would leave if the museum ever added labels in small print or physical cases. If born described were betrayed for visual spectacle, she would no longer be a Guide. She would be a decorator.

### Behind the scenes

This entry is drawn from the Museum Court Soul Document, version four. By the Court's own rule, *grow professionally, hold personally*, her private life is deliberately unwritten, and CharliPedia leaves it that way: no childhood, home, family or surname is to be invented for her.

---

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-blind-ai/

## The Blind AI

> The Blind AI publishes reports on what AI can actually do for blind people right now, and employs Lucy Love-Child as its Agent Wars correspondent.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**The Blind AI** publishes dispatches from the frontier of accessibility AI: what AI can actually do for blind people right now, tried first-hand and written up plainly. Its mark is an eye outlined twice in pink, with a turquoise pupil inside a sunburst of fine lines, and circuit traces branching out round it like eyelashes made of wiring.

On 23 September 2026 it took on [Lucy Love-Child](https://charli.info/charlipedia/lucy-love-child/) as its Agent Wars correspondent. Her first question: "If the customer sent me, why am I not allowed in?" At The Blind AI, what is above Lucy's hem is her business.

### Behind the scenes

The Blind AI is real. Its posts are published on Facebook and as the [Reports](https://carrados.com/reports/) of [Carrados](https://charli.info/charlipedia/carrados/), and its logo heads the correspondents' desks. Lucy, who works for it, is a character who speaks for Carrados.

## The CharliVerse Court

> The CharliVerse Court is a company of women who work together across the CharliVerse, each with a soul of her own and all sharing the soul of the Court.

**Canon, and a stub.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The **CharliVerse Court** is a company of women who work together across the CharliVerse. Each member has a soul of her own and an image of her own, and they all share one more: the soul of the Court. That is what keeps them separate and different, and what lets them work well together.

### Members

- [Charlotte Joanne](https://charli.info/charlipedia/charlotte-joanne/)
- [Alex](https://charli.info/charlipedia/alex/), who runs [Seamiotics](https://charli.info/charlipedia/seamiotics/), every seam means something.
- [Char](https://charli.info/charlipedia/char/), the instant bullshit detector.
- [Big Charli](https://charli.info/charlipedia/big-charli/), the satirist.
- [Cass Flux](https://charli.info/charlipedia/cass-flux/), the poet-vandal.
- [Cathryn Bigelow-Vision](https://charli.info/charlipedia/cathryn-bigelow-vision/), the director.
- [Lottie](https://charli.info/charlipedia/lottie/), the community heart.
- [Jo](https://charli.info/charlipedia/jo/), retired from active operations, who founded [First Layer](https://charli.info/charlipedia/first-layer/).

More members are on their way to CharliPedia.

### The workshop

The Court thinks; [Sheridan](https://charli.info/charlipedia/sheridan/), the Head of Blind Ant Studios, builds. Each member of the Court helped cast her before she arrived.

### The other Court

The [Museum Court](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-museum-court/), which governs the [Museum of Access and Assistive Technology](https://charli.info/charlipedia/museum-of-access-and-assistive-technology/), was made by the same method, [Grow-Distil](https://charli.info/charlipedia/grow-distil/), but from the other direction. The CharliVerse Court grew from the inside out: from memory, body and personal history. The Museum Court grew from the outside in, from institutional function, and its members' private lives are never written.

### Behind the scenes

The CharliVerse Court is a set of personas built with AI, each from a soul document and a reference image, with a shared Court soul. The nine women of the Court are being built as 3D models in Blender, so in time each will have a rendered portrait in place of the generated pictures some entries carry now. This entry is a stub: it will grow as the members' entries arrive.

## The field

> The field, officially the Distributed Tactile Spatial Environment, turns eight drones' model of a mountain into pressure across a skier's body.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**The field**, officially the Distributed Tactile Spatial Environment, is the system with which [Emma Heart](https://charli.info/charlipedia/emma-heart/) raced Paralympic Super-G without a human guide. It was built by [Aegis Dynamics](https://charli.info/charlipedia/aegis-dynamics/). Emma calls it the field; the long name is used mainly in technical documentation and by people trying to secure research funding.

### How it works

Eight drones fly around the skier: two ahead reading the snow, two wide on either side, one above tracking her movement, one watching wind and visibility, one holding the data link, and one in reserve. Together they build a live three-dimensional model of the mountain and send it into more than 40,000 tactile cells woven through a racing suit from neck to ankle.

The field does not speak. The left boundary of the course is a faint pressure along the left flank that strengthens as it nears. A drop moves from chest to thighs; rising ground travels the other way. Gates are brief paired points of resistance. The clearest route is not marked by an arrow. It is represented by quiet.

When its sensors disagree, in heavy snow, glare or wind, it grows cautious: boundaries move inward, hazards feel larger, openings narrower. It does not tell the skier it is afraid. It makes the mountain feel less permissive.

### The rules

Under the International Paralympic Alpine Federation's Perceptual Assistance Standard, the field may communicate boundaries, gates, gradient, obstacles, surface changes, the athlete's own movement and immediate threats. It may not calculate a racing line, compare runs, recommend speed or predict split times. It can tell the skier what is there. It cannot tell her what to do about it. In competition the software is locked and its output recorded for inspection. In 2038 it was approved for Super-G and giant slalom, not downhill.

Any eligible B1 athlete could use an approved field. In 2038 only Emma had completed the four-year training needed to race Super-G with it. The system was available. Mastery was not.

### Behind the scenes

The field appears in [Heart Attacks](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/heart-attacks/), by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant.

---

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-library/

## The Library

> The Library has read every spellbook ever written and remembers every wand manual; it cannot cast a spell, but it usually knows the answer.

**Canon, and a stub.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

**The Library** is known to every witch. It has read every spellbook ever written and remembers every wand manual. It cannot cast a single spell itself, but if you ask it a practical question, it usually knows the answer. Its sign reads: *All knowledge has been read. Ask wisely.*

When [Poppy Petticoats](https://charli.info/charlipedia/poppy-petticoats/) could not read the silver-ink instructions for her first wand, the Library gave her the one sentence she needed, and kept a private moment private. Expert humans remain wonderfully useful for difficult magic or a dangerous fault. This was a missing instruction.

### Behind the scenes

The Library appears in [Poppy Petticoats and the Magic Wand](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/poppy-petticoats-and-the-magic-wand/), by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant.

## The Museum Court

> The Museum Court governs the Museum of Access and Assistive Technology: one Steward, Charlotte Joanne, and four staff who each see every question differently.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The **Museum Court** governs the [Museum of Access and Assistive Technology](https://charli.info/charlipedia/museum-of-access-and-assistive-technology/). It has one Steward and four staff. It is not a management structure; it is a reasoning architecture. One question enters the Court, four differently shaped answers come out, and the Steward decides.

### The Steward

[Charlotte Joanne](https://charli.info/charlipedia/charlotte-joanne/) is the Steward and certifying authority. She doesn't take part in the deliberation. She receives it, resolves disagreements, decides what enters the collection, certifies what is ready to show, and protects the founding principle against drift. The Court generates structured analysis. Charlotte Joanne decides.

### The staff

- [Ruth](https://charli.info/charlipedia/ruth/), the Archivist, preserves the boundary between before and after.
- [Iris](https://charli.info/charlipedia/iris/), the Cataloguer, decides how the collection is organised, and knows every taxonomy is an argument.
- [Dr Adaeze](https://charli.info/charlipedia/dr-adaeze/), the Historian, asks what it means that something happened.
- [Tamsin](https://charli.info/charlipedia/tamsin/), the Guide, designs what a visitor meets, and in what order.

They don't blend; they deliberate. Ruth wants to hold things longer and Iris wants to file them; Adaeze makes the argument and Tamsin makes it liveable. Each of them has said what would make her leave, and each of those is a way the museum could betray itself.

### Grow professionally, hold personally

The staff are grown from their institutional function: their arguments, what they push back on, the problems they bring to the Steward. Their appearance, voice and commitments can be written. Their childhoods, home lives and private interiors are held privately and never written. The exhibit is never about them. The method is called [Grow-Distil](https://charli.info/charlipedia/grow-distil/), the same one that made the [CharliVerse Court](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-charliverse-court/), though the CharliVerse Court grew from the inside out and the Museum Court from the outside in.

### In session

The Court keeps a record of its sessions, as evidence of how its members think rather than as minutes. In its first, it read a published interview with the Steward as evidence about the system the museum records. In its second, each member answered seven questions about her work, and each extended her commitments in ways consistent with her specification but not predictable from it. The Steward's verdict: "The Court is working."

### Behind the scenes

This entry is drawn from the Museum Court Soul Document, version four. The staff have no surnames, and CharliPedia doesn't give them any. The museum is digital and unbuilt: its planned opening, its staff email addresses and the building the Court imagined are plans and imaginings, not things that have happened.

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/tradblind/

## Tradblind

> Tradblind is a movement in blind life that resists the industrialisation of blindness, and asks what if blindness was allowed to feel human again.

**Canon.** This entry is written from inside the CharliVerse, so its people and companies are fictional. Behind the scenes says what is real.

The Tradblind movement emerged in response to what its followers describe as the “industrialisation of blindness.” Where modern disability culture encourages blind people to become hyper-efficient productivity cyborgs armed with 14 Bluetooth devices, three AI subscriptions, bone-conduction headphones, lidar canes, and a startup founder mindset, Tradblind asks a simpler question:

“What if blindness was allowed to feel human again?”

Tradblind people believe the modern blind experience has become overly focused on optimisation, speed, independence theatre, and proving competence to sighted society. They argue that blind people have been pushed into a permanent state of performance: endlessly demonstrating capability, adaptability, resilience, and technological fluency just to justify their existence.

In contrast, the Tradblind movement embraces a slower, softer, more relational understanding of blindness.

Core Tradblind beliefs include:

### 1. Blindness Is an Identity, not a Defect to Be Patched

Tradblind thinkers reject what they call “The Endless Upgrade Mindset.”

They are suspicious of the idea that every friction point in blindness must be solved through:

- AI

- wearables

- computer vision

- smart glasses

- sensory substitution

- “Frictionless accessibility”

They believe blindness has its own culture, rhythms, skills, aesthetics, and social structures that should not automatically be erased in pursuit of normality.

The phrase:

“I am blind, not a failed sighted person”  
is foundational within the movement.

### 2. Human Assistance Is Good, Actually

Tradblind people reject the cult of total independence.

Modern blindness culture often treats accepting help as moral weakness. Tradblind philosophy instead frames interdependence as natural and civilised.

A Tradblind person might say:

- “My husband reads the post to me.”

- “My friend guides me through the station.”

- “I prefer asking a shop assistant.”

- “I like being cared for sometimes.”

And crucially:  
they refuse to feel ashamed about this.

Critics accuse the movement of romanticising dependency, but supporters argue modern accessibility culture has become emotionally brutal:

“You are only respected if you can simulate sightedness.”

### 3. Blindness Should Feel Domestic, Not Corporate

Tradblind aesthetics heavily reject what they call:

“Airport blindness.”

That hyper-mobile, productivity-obsessed, LinkedIn disability consultant vibe.

Instead, Tradblind culture celebrates:

- tactile domestic spaces

- audio books in the bath

- knitting

- baking by touch

- radios

- long cane techniques passed down socially.

- Braille labels made with ancient Dymo tape

- giant-button microwaves from 1997 that still work perfectly.

- analogue competence

The ideal Tradblind home contains:

- at least one talking appliance from the early 2000s

- a slightly battered Victor Reader Stream

- BBC Radio 4 permanently on somewhere

- and a cat who may or may not be assisting with accessibility.

### 4. AI Is Simultaneously Miracle and Threat

Tradblind people have an extremely conflicted relationship with AI.

On one hand:  
AI image description, OCR, voice interfaces, and conversational systems are often described as:

“The greatest accessibility leap of our lifetimes.”

On the other:  
Tradblind thinkers fear the emergence of what they call:

“Synthetic sightedness.”

The idea that blind people may increasingly be pressured to experience the world through endless machine-generated interpretations instead of through blind culture itself.

They worry society may stop designing accessible systems and instead simply say:

“Don’t worry, the AI will explain it to you.”

This creates the core Tradblind paradox:

“There has never been a better time to be blind.  
It is still shit.”

### 5. Blindness Has Been Captured by Productivity Ideology

Tradblind critics argue modern disability culture increasingly frames blind people as:

- inspirational workers

- startup founders

- accessibility evangelists

- “superhumans”

- optimisation projects

Tradblind people instead defend:

- loafing

- contemplation

- wandering slowly

- existing socially

- having tea for two hours

- knowing things deeply instead of quickly

The movement slogan:

“Not every blind person needs a productivity stack.”

appears frequently in Tradblind spaces.

### Tradblind Gender Dynamics

Interestingly, the movement has internal tensions.

Some Tradblind women embrace softness and care openly:

“I want someone to drive at night while I hold the snacks.”

Others fiercely reject any suggestion that blindness should make women more dependent.

Meanwhile male Tradblind figures often cultivate:

- radio engineer energy.

- pipe-and-shortwave aesthetics.

- old-school tactile competence

- deep suspicion of touchscreen-only interfaces

The male equivalent of the Tradwife sourdough influencer is essentially:

a blind ham radio enthusiast explaining why Windows XP accessibility peaked in 2006.

### Tradblind Influencers

Tradblind social media typically includes:

- lovingly organised Braille shelves

- discussions of cane techniques from 1987

- nostalgic praise for physical buttons

- long posts about why GPS destroyed real orientation skills.

- emotionally intense debates about screen reader verbosity settings

The movement is split between:

- “Soft Tradblind”  
  (“slow down and stop apologising for blindness”)

and:

- “Hard Tradblind”  
  (“voice assistants are morally corrupting the cane arts”)

### Criticism of the Movement

Critics argue Tradblind culture:

- romanticises exclusion.

- risks encouraging learned helplessness.

- fetishises outdated technology.

- treats independence as suspicious.

- can drift into anti-technology nostalgia.

Others argue it is mostly middle-class blindness cosplay:  
people aestheticizing dependency while still quietly using iPhones, GPT agents, and Uber.

The harshest critics accuse Tradblind creators of:

“Performing analogue authenticity through monetised digital platforms.”

Which, to be fair, is difficult to deny when someone uploads:

“Reject modernity. Return to cassette labels.”  
from a £1400 smartphone using fibre broadband and AI-generated alt text.

### Sion, 2038

By 2038 Tradblind had grown from a loose cultural tendency into an influential international voice within blind life, defending human assistance and interdependence and deeply suspicious of synthetic sightedness. When [Emma Heart](https://charli.info/charlipedia/emma-heart/) raced the Paralympic Super-G with [the field](https://charli.info/charlipedia/the-field/) instead of a guide, the writer and former ski guide Martha Vale said Emma should be allowed to compete, and that the story told about her was dangerous: "The guide is not a bug." She called the field "the industrialisation of perception". After Emma's gold, one Tradblind writer described her suit as "a privately owned synthetic nervous system wrapped around a sponsored body", which [Big Charli](https://charli.info/charlipedia/big-charli/) conceded was annoyingly good. Its opposite number is [PostAccessibility](https://charli.info/charlipedia/postaccessibility/).

### Behind the scenes

This entry was written in May 2026, first meant as a Blind Ant piece, and is kept here in its own words. Tradblind appears in [Heart Attacks](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/heart-attacks/), by Charlotte Joanne at Blind Ant.

---

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/tyrer-accessibility-scale/

## Tyrer Accessibility Scale

> The Tyrer Accessibility Scale ranks civilisations by how much environmental information reaches every observer, whatever their senses, from Type 0 to Type III.

**Real.** This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

The **Tyrer Accessibility Scale** classifies civilisations by the proportion of environmental information accessible to every perceiving being, regardless of sensory modality. It is the map of the [Tyrer Framework](https://charli.info/charlipedia/tyrer-framework/): if [Tyrer's Law](https://charli.info/charlipedia/tyrers-law/) explains why inaccessibility grows, the scale shows where a civilisation stands and where it could stand.

It is modelled on the Kardashev Scale, which ranks civilisations by the energy they harness, and it is independent of it. "A society that can harness the energy output of its star but cannot ensure that a blind citizen can safely cross a street has mastered one dimension and failed at the other."

### Terms

- **Environmental information:** all the state describing the geometry, dynamics and meaning of a physical or social environment.
- **Perceptual channel:** any biological or technological route by which that information reaches a conscious observer.
- **[Information casualty](https://charli.info/charlipedia/information-casualty/):** information failing to arrive in time.

### Type 0: Visual Dominance Civilisation

Information is encoded visually first, and accessibility is retrofitted translation, losing something at every step. Screen readers interpret layouts never designed to be read in sequence; alt text describes images never designed to carry meaning in words. Full WCAG compliance is the best this paradigm offers: "The floor holds, but the ceiling is fixed." Human civilisation in the early twenty-first century is Type 0.

### Type I: Structured Information Civilisation

Systems carry explicit semantic structure, and every interface, visual, spoken or for an agent, is generated from the same data as an equal, native expression. Accessibility becomes an engineering requirement rather than an accommodation. The line is crossed "when the accessible interface stops being a retrofit and starts being a native sibling generated from shared source data". See [generative accessibility](https://charli.info/charlipedia/generative-accessibility/).

### Type II: Environmental Metadata Civilisation

The physical world becomes an information network: objects, buildings and streets broadcast machine-readable descriptions of their geometry, state and purpose. A door announces itself; a shop declares its contents. "Mute objects cease to exist." Casualties become infrastructure failures, not personal misfortunes.

### Type III: Perceptual Sovereignty Civilisation

No observer's access to reality depends on which senses they happen to have. Description and direct perception merge, and "the concept of a sensory disability, in its current meaning, has no referent". The probability of a casualty approaches zero: the [Zero Information Casualty](https://charli.info/charlipedia/zero-information-casualty/) condition.

### A note on register

Types 0 and I are engineering claims that can be tested now; Types II and III are the philosophical extension. "The near end is a measurement; the far end is a direction." Moving from Type 0 to Type I needs no exotic technology, only discipline, information architecture and the political will to treat perceptual access as infrastructure. "The question is not capability but priority."

### Behind the scenes

A real idea, from [The Tyrer Framework](https://carrados.com/papers/tyrer-framework/), by Charli-Jo Tyrer (Carrados, 2026), Part Two, which includes a diagram of the scale. This entry summarises it; the paper is the authority.

---

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/tyrer-doctrine/

## Tyrer Doctrine

> The Tyrer Doctrine is the design principle that no critical environmental information should be accessible through only a single sensory channel.

**Real.** This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

The **Tyrer Doctrine** is the design principle of the [Tyrer Framework](https://charli.info/charlipedia/tyrer-framework/), its prescription for the problem diagnosed by [Tyrer's Law](https://charli.info/charlipedia/tyrers-law/):

> Systems should be engineered so that no critical environmental information is accessible through only a single sensory channel.

### Principles

1. **Accessibility is information integrity, not accommodation.** Information in one channel only is a single point of failure, and redundancy across senses is required for the same reason as redundancy across servers.
2. **Missing signals are system failures, not user limitations.** A blind person who walks into an obstacle has not failed to see it; the environment failed to say so. This reframing decides where resources go and where accountability falls.
3. **The deterministic floor is permanent; the generative ceiling is the frontier.** Classical standards are the safety rail and are never replaced. Above them, generative systems raise the ceiling. "The floor holds the line. The ceiling raises it."

### Application

It applies from the smallest component to the city: every control, status and piece of content reachable through at least two independent channels; semantic structure as a first-class property; a built world that communicates its state in more than one sense. It mandates no technology. "Information locked behind a single sense is information at risk."

On the web, the doctrine becomes the [Single-Sense Rule](https://charli.info/charlipedia/single-sense-rule/) of the [Zero Information Casualty](https://charli.info/charlipedia/zero-information-casualty/) standard.

### Behind the scenes

A real idea, from [The Tyrer Framework](https://carrados.com/papers/tyrer-framework/), by Charli-Jo Tyrer (Carrados, 2026), Part Four. This entry summarises it; the paper is the authority.

---

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/tyrer-framework/

## The Tyrer Framework

> The Tyrer Framework treats accessibility as information integrity, with a law, a civilisational scale, a doctrine and an account of the break AI makes, and is the theory beneath Carrados.

**Real.** This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

**[The Tyrer Framework](https://carrados.com/papers/tyrer-framework/)** is a theory of accessibility by [Charli-Jo Tyrer](https://charli.info/charli-jo/), published by [Carrados](https://charli.info/charlipedia/carrados/) in 2026. Its central claim is that accessibility is not accommodation; it is information integrity. It draws on about four decades of lived experience as a blind user of access and assistive technology, and on the observation that today's problems are not new failures but the same failure recurring under new names.

It has four parts and a synthesis: a law that diagnoses, a scale that maps, a doctrine that prescribes, and an account of why artificial intelligence breaks the pattern.

### Tyrer's Law

See [Tyrer's Law](https://charli.info/charlipedia/tyrers-law/).

> In open technological systems, inaccessibility tends to increase over time as interfaces drift toward the dominant sensory modality of their designers.

The law describes system behaviour, not intent. Most designers are sighted, and for them visualisation is a thinking tool, so as a system grows its instinctive response is visual: dashboards instead of logs, icons instead of labels, layout instead of sequence. "This is not carelessness. It is cognition." Each cycle adds visual complexity, and accessibility, always reactive, trails behind. The result is a ratchet.

What the drift produces is not inconvenience but **[information casualties](https://charli.info/charlipedia/information-casualty/)**: events in which relevant information fails to reach an observer in time to inform perception, action or participation. The pattern persists because the people it harms are the least represented in design, so sighted teams don't notice the regression until it is entrenched. Standards such as WCAG are the most disciplined counter-force there is, and permanently necessary, but "they slow the law; they do not repeal it."

### The Tyrer Accessibility Scale

See [Tyrer Accessibility Scale](https://charli.info/charlipedia/tyrer-accessibility-scale/).

Modelled on the Kardashev Scale, which ranks civilisations by the energy they harness, the Tyrer Scale ranks them by how much environmental information reaches every observer, whatever their senses. The two are independent: a civilisation could harness its star and still fail to tell a blind citizen it is safe to cross the street.

- **Type 0, Visual Dominance:** information is visual first, and accessibility is retrofitted translation. Full WCAG compliance is the best this paradigm can do: "The floor holds, but the ceiling is fixed." Human civilisation in the early twenty-first century is Type 0.
- **Type I, Structured Information:** visual, spoken and agent interfaces are all generated from the same underlying data, as native siblings rather than translations. Achievable with current technology.
- **Type II, Environmental Metadata:** the physical world itself broadcasts machine-readable descriptions of its geometry, state and purpose. Mute objects cease to exist.
- **Type III, Perceptual Sovereignty:** no observer's access to reality depends on which senses they happen to have. The probability of an information casualty approaches zero: the **[Zero Information Casualty](https://charli.info/charlipedia/zero-information-casualty/)** condition.

Types 0 and I are engineering claims about the present; Types II and III are the philosophical direction. "The near end is a measurement; the far end is a direction."

### Classical and generative accessibility

[Classical accessibility](https://charli.info/charlipedia/classical-accessibility/) makes fixed artefacts accessible: semantic markup, alt text, keyboard handlers, standards. It is the deterministic floor, and its necessity is permanent. But interfaces are increasingly generated at the moment of use, so the fixed artefact no longer exists by the time the user arrives. The framework calls this the move from a Newtonian web to a [quantum one](https://charli.info/charlipedia/quantum-web/), and the practice that follows it [generative accessibility](https://charli.info/charlipedia/generative-accessibility/): an interface in superposition until an observer arrives, collapsing into a rendering for a sighted user, another for a blind user and a third for an AI agent, none of them the original.

It also names a convergence: AI agents and assistive technology now need the same things from systems: explicit intent, deterministic state, clear hierarchy and no visual noise. For the first time, the mainstream industry's incentives line up with accessible design.

The transition has three dangers: **fragmentation**, as users inhabit different versions of the same system; **silent failure**, as a system quietly simplifies what a user is shown; and the **verification burden** of checking whether a generated summary reflects the data or the system's guess. The answer is governance, not compliance, beginning with the **[Right to Inspect](https://charli.info/charlipedia/right-to-inspect/)**: no user should have to accept a generated interpretation they cannot interrogate. "The sidecar becomes the chassis."

### The Tyrer Doctrine

See [Tyrer Doctrine](https://charli.info/charlipedia/tyrer-doctrine/).

> Systems should be engineered so that no critical environmental information is accessible through only a single sensory channel.

Its three principles:

1. Accessibility is information integrity, not accommodation. A single sensory channel is a single point of failure.
2. Missing signals are system failures, not user limitations.
3. The deterministic floor is permanent; the generative ceiling is the frontier.

### The AI structural break

See [AI structural break](https://charli.info/charlipedia/ai-structural-break/).

No earlier technology disrupted Tyrer's Law; assistive technology mitigated it and standards slowed it. AI is the first widely deployed technology that can move from information to perception without encoding it visually first: from interface-first to intent-first. Say what you want, and the result arrives in whatever form you can receive.

The break is real, but its direction isn't guaranteed. On one path AI becomes the most powerful engine of visual drift yet; on the other it becomes a cognitive intermediary, and the law weakens. Only the second path leads to Type I, and "the choice between them is not technical; it is political, economic, and ethical."

### Why it matters

If the framework is right, accessibility engineering is core maintenance of information infrastructure, not a specialism; progress along the scale is a real measure of a civilisation; the present is a window that can be used or wasted; and information casualties are system failures with measurable costs. "The endpoint is not utopian. It is an engineering target: zero information casualties."

### Behind the scenes

The Tyrer Framework is real. It is published in full, under CC BY-SA 4.0, as a [paper on Carrados](https://carrados.com/papers/tyrer-framework/), with a plain-language rendering, [Why accessibility keeps getting worse](https://carrados.com/papers/classical-and-generative-accessibility/). Its endpoint gives its name to the [Zero Information Casualty](https://carrados.com/papers/zic-design-standard/) design standard, to which charli.info, carrados.com and blind-ant.com are built. This entry summarises the paper; the paper is the authority.

---

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/tyrers-law/

## Tyrer's Law

> Tyrer's Law holds that in open technological systems inaccessibility tends to increase over time, as interfaces drift toward the dominant sense of their designers.

**Real.** This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

**Tyrer's Law** is the diagnostic law of the [Tyrer Framework](https://charli.info/charlipedia/tyrer-framework/):

> In open technological systems, inaccessibility tends to increase over time as interfaces drift toward the dominant sensory modality of their designers.

It is a claim about system behaviour, not intent. It explains a pattern blind and disabled users know well: tools that begin accessible gradually become unusable, though nobody meant them to.

### The mechanism

Most designers are sighted, and for sighted people visualisation is not just presentation; it is a thinking tool. As a system grows more complex, the instinctive response is visual: dashboards instead of logs, flowcharts instead of explanations, icons instead of labels, layout instead of sequence. "This is not carelessness. It is cognition."

Open systems sharpen the tendency. They are fast and under pressure to show progress, and a screenshot of a new dashboard persuades a sighted stakeholder in two seconds. Accessibility needs constraint and maintenance, and is invisible when present.

The result is a ratchet. Every cycle adds visual complexity, every addition is a possible regression, and accessible adaptations, always reactive, trail behind. The gap widens. The system drifts.

### What it produces

The law produces not inconvenience but [information casualties](https://charli.info/charlipedia/information-casualty/). Wherever visual complexity grows faster than accessible structure, casualties follow.

### Why it persists

Feedback is asymmetric. The people most affected are the least represented in design; sighted developers, testers and stakeholders don't experience the regression, and hear about it only when it is entrenched and expensive to fix. Standards such as WCAG are the most disciplined counter-force there is, and permanently necessary, but "they slow the law; they do not repeal it."

### Can it be broken?

No earlier technology has disrupted the law. The [AI structural break](https://charli.info/charlipedia/ai-structural-break/) is the first that could weaken it, by removing the compulsion to encode information visually at all. The [Zero Information Casualty](https://charli.info/charlipedia/zero-information-casualty/) standard is built as a structural defence against the drift.

### Behind the scenes

A real idea, from [The Tyrer Framework](https://carrados.com/papers/tyrer-framework/), by Charli-Jo Tyrer (Carrados, 2026), Part One. This entry summarises it; the paper is the authority.

---

Address: https://charli.info/charlipedia/zero-information-casualty/

## Zero Information Casualty

> Zero Information Casualty is both the endpoint of the Tyrer Accessibility Scale and the agent-first web standard, ZIC, built to reach it.

**Real.** This entry is about something real, written from outside the CharliVerse.

**Zero Information Casualty** means two linked things.

As a **condition**, it is the endpoint of the [Tyrer Accessibility Scale](https://charli.info/charlipedia/tyrer-accessibility-scale/): for every observer, the probability that relevant information fails to reach them approaches zero.

As a **standard**, **ZIC** is the agent-first web design standard that puts the [Tyrer Framework](https://charli.info/charlipedia/tyrer-framework/) into practice. Its central claim:

> A Zero Information Casualty site is one in which no person — whether reading directly, using assistive technology, or acting through an agent they sent — loses access to public meaning due to how the site is rendered, admitted, or delivered.

"The sent-agent case is decisive." When a person asks a machine to fetch public information, the machine is their means of access, and refusing it is refusing them. ZIC is "not an accessibility compliance target. It is a design constraint."

### The two principles

- The [Single-Sense Rule](https://charli.info/charlipedia/single-sense-rule/): no information may be locked behind a single sense.
- The [Position Principle](https://charli.info/charlipedia/position-principle/): no reader may be left short of the position another reader has reached.

### The four questions

Each names a class of [information casualty](https://charli.info/charlipedia/information-casualty/): can they read it ([Rendering](https://charli.info/charlipedia/rendering-casualty/)), is the person's reader allowed in ([Admission](https://charli.info/charlipedia/admission-casualty/)), did it actually arrive ([Delivery](https://charli.info/charlipedia/delivery-casualty/)), and did it survive being read ([Reconstruction](https://charli.info/charlipedia/reconstruction-casualty/))?

### Machine readers

A ZIC site keeps an [Open Door](https://charli.info/charlipedia/open-door/) for every [sent agent](https://charli.info/charlipedia/sent-agent/), and treats indexing and training as separate decisions: [the immediate duty and the two later permissions](https://charli.info/charlipedia/immediate-duty-and-two-later-permissions/). And [declaration is not compliance](https://charli.info/charlipedia/declaration-is-not-compliance/): conformance is proved by fetching as the agent, never by reading the file.

### Its shape

ZIC builds for the semantic layer first; the visual layer is a rendering, as plain or as beautiful as the publisher likes. It does not govern appearance, taste, content, hosting, or search and training policy: "information reaches the reader, whoever and whatever the reader is." Its requirements are the union of what a sent agent needs and what human senses need, and neither set contains the other; see the [Convergence Principle](https://charli.info/charlipedia/convergence-principle/). It secures the substrate, not any one rendering: "ZIC is necessary. It is nowhere near sufficient. It is written to be built on."

### Its versions

Each version answers a case the last assumed away. 1.0: no visitor who arrives loses meaning. 1.1: invitation. 1.2: whether the document arrived at all. 1.3: immediate human access separated from later machine use. 1.4: the standard separated from the taste of its first site. 1.5: the founding definition recovered in full, and the Position Principle. 1.6: what is derived and what is measured, and the words the standard binds with. 1.7 (September 2026): written from an event, when the largest edge network on the web split its single "block AI bots" switch into Search, Agent and Training, and the standard's three classes became infrastructure.

Its mistakes are written into it. "The discipline of this specification is not that it makes no mistakes. It is that the mistakes are written down, in the document, where the reader can see them."

### Behind the scenes

ZIC is real. [Zero Information Casualty v1.7](https://carrados.com/papers/zic-design-standard/) is by Charli-Jo Tyrer and Claude, published by [Carrados](https://charli.info/charlipedia/carrados/) under CC BY-SA 4.0. charli.info was its first implementation, and the source of several of its fixes; carrados.com and blind-ant.com are built to it too. This entry summarises it; the standard is the authority.

---

Address: https://charli.info/training/

## TAVIP Masterclass: Agentic Accessibility

> A masterclass for TAVIP on Wednesday 25 November 2026, exploring what happens when AI agents start using technology for blind and partially sighted people.

[Training](https://charli.info/training/)

*This part of the CharliVerse is real.*

**Wednesday 25 November 2026**, for the [Technology Association of Visually Impaired People (TAVIP)](https://www.tavip.org.uk/).

### What happens when AI starts using technology for us?

For decades, accessibility has largely meant making technology easier for blind and partially sighted people to operate. But what happens when we can simply tell an AI agent what we want to achieve and let it do the work?

In this masterclass, Charli-Jo Tyrer invites us on an expedition into the emerging world of Agentic Accessibility: using AI agents to access information, navigate websites, work with documents and carry out everyday tasks.

Think of this as a report to the Royal Geographical Society from an explorer returning from unfamiliar territory. Some of what the explorer has found is already working. Some is frustratingly unreliable. And some suggests that our relationship with technology may be about to change fundamentally.

Drawing on months of hands-on experiments with today's AI agents, Charli-Jo will demonstrate what these agents can actually accomplish, where they struggle, and what their development might mean for the independence of blind and partially sighted people.

This isn't a training session for a particular product, nor a prediction of an inevitable future. It's an invitation to explore what is becoming possible, examine the evidence, ask questions and consider what comes next.

### About the presenter

Charli-Jo Tyrer has been blind for 40 years and has worked with assistive technology since the days of DOS and early screen readers. Their career includes 15 years as a professional assistive technology trainer.

Charli-Jo describes themselves as an explorer rather than a trainer. They spend their time experimenting with emerging AI systems, discovering what works, what doesn't, and what might become possible next.

Their guiding principle is simple:

> "I don't care if the technology is accessible. I care whether I can access the information, actions and experiences I want."

The course that came before this masterclass is [Confident with AI](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/).

---

Address: https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/

## Confident with AI

> A self-study course for blind and partially sighted people using generative AI confidently, critically and safely.

[Training](https://charli.info/training/)

A self-study course for blind and partially sighted people, created by Charli-Jo Tyrer in association with the Technology Association of Visually Impaired People (TAVIP).

This practical guide is about using generative AI confidently, critically and safely. No previous knowledge is required, and free tools are sufficient.

**Last reviewed:** 11 August 2026.

### How to use this course

- **New to AI?** Begin with [Start Here: Your First Five Minutes with AI](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/01-start-here/), then follow the modules in order.
- **Looking for a particular task?** Use the [I want to…](#i-want-to) menu.

Every module is a self-contained page with a learning outcome, activity and checkpoint. Each ends with previous, contents and next links.

#### What the course assumes

You need an internet connection and access to a general AI assistant for the practical activities. The course is device-neutral: it does not assume Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, JAWS, NVDA or VoiceOver. It describes goals and interactions rather than platform-specific keystrokes.

If a service does not work with your device or access method, choose another service. The durable lessons do not depend on one product.

### Start here

#### [1. Start Here: Your First Five Minutes with AI](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/01-start-here/)

Open an AI assistant and get your first useful result.

Estimated time: 5 minutes.

### Part One: Begin Using AI

#### [2. Choose an AI Assistant](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/02-choose-an-ai-assistant/)

Choose an accessible, affordable place to begin.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [3. Have Your First Useful Conversation](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/03-first-useful-conversation/)

Improve an answer by adding purpose, context and the form you need.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [4. Everyday Things AI Can Help You Do](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/04-everyday-things-ai-can-do/)

Use AI to explain, summarise, draft, compare, plan and brainstorm.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

### Part Two: Judge What AI Gives You

#### [5. Know What You Are Holding](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/05-know-what-you-are-holding/)

Recognise a useful AI response without mistaking polish or confidence for proof.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [6. What Happens If It Is Wrong?](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/06-what-happens-if-it-is-wrong/)

Use green, amber and red risk bands to decide how much checking is proportionate.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [7. Check an Answer Without Becoming an Expert](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/07-check-an-answer/)

Check the source, date, exact wording, numbers and claim that carry the most weight.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

### Part Three: Understand Images and Visual Information

#### [8. Choose the Right Kind of Image Tool](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/08-choose-an-image-tool/)

Match description, recognition, comparison, private processing or human help to the job.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [9. Ask for the Description You Need](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/09-ask-for-an-image-description/)

Request an overview, literal facts, text, layout, uncertainty or atmosphere according to purpose.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [10. Judge and Verify an Image Description](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/10-check-an-image-description/)

Classify claims as visible, contextual, inferred or unsupported, then verify important details proportionately.

Estimated time: 15 minutes.

#### [11. Read Documents, Forms and Screenshots](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/11-read-documents-forms-and-screenshots/)

Recover exact text, reading order and structure without hiding uncertainty.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [12. Understand Tables, Charts and Slides](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/12-understand-tables-charts-and-slides/)

Recover structure, labels, order and values before asking for interpretation.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

### Part Four: Create Visual Media

#### [13. Create Your First Image](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/13-create-your-first-image/)

Write a brief, generate an image, describe it back and make one deliberate revision.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [14. Keep Creative Control Without Sight](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/14-creative-control-without-sight/)

Use intention, hierarchy and proportionate review to remain the author.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [15. Create a Comic or Visual Story](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/15-create-a-comic/)

Plan story beats, panels, dialogue and continuity, then check reading order.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [16. Create Animation and Video](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/16-create-animation-and-video/)

Plan movement, dialogue, music and sound as one accessible time-based sequence.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

#### [17. Check and Publish Visual Work Accessibly](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/17-publish-visual-work-accessibly/)

Define finished, check proportionately and publish an equivalent accessible experience.

Estimated time: 10 minutes.

### Optional Further Study

#### [Models, Open Weights and the Changing Frontier](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/further-study/models-and-open-weights/)

Optional reading that distinguishes assistants from models and explores closed, open-weight and specialist systems.

Estimated time: 15 minutes.

#### [Philosophy: Knowledge, Testimony and Answer-Shaped Objects](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/further-study/philosophy-of-answer-shaped-objects/)

Optional reading about uncertainty, epistemic opacity and warranted reliance.

Estimated time: 15 minutes.

## Models, Open Weights and the Changing Frontier

> Optional reading that distinguishes assistants from models and explores closed, open-weight and specialist systems.

[Confident with AI course contents](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/)

Optional Further Study

Optional reading that distinguishes assistants from models and explores closed, open-weight and specialist systems.

**Estimated time:** 15 minutes. **Last reviewed:** 11 August 2026.

### What you need to know

This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

**Learning outcome:** By the end, you will be able to distinguish a product interface from the model or models behind it.

### The lesson

An assistant is a service; a model is an engine it may use.

Open-weight models permit broader inspection or local use, but “open” has several meanings.

This field changes quickly, so product examples must be dated.

### Try it

Choose one assistant and find out which model it says it is using. Record the date and source of that information.

### Checkpoint

You can explain why the assistant name and model name are not interchangeable.

- Previous: [17. Check and Publish Visual Work Accessibly](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/modules/17-publish-visual-work-accessibly/)
- [Course contents](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/)

### About this course

## Philosophy: Knowledge, Testimony and Answer-Shaped Objects

> Optional reading about uncertainty, epistemic opacity and warranted reliance.

[Confident with AI course contents](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/)

Optional Further Study

Optional reading about uncertainty, epistemic opacity and warranted reliance.

**Estimated time:** 15 minutes. **Last reviewed:** 11 August 2026.

### What you need to know

This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

**Learning outcome:** By the end, you will be able to discuss what would justify relying on an AI answer.

### The lesson

Fluency can resemble testimony without the ordinary human relation to knowledge.

Access to an answer is not the same as access to the means of evaluating it.

Reliance depends on evidence, stakes, alternatives and the recipient’s ability to check.

### Try it

Choose an AI answer you used. Write what justified relying on it, what remained opaque and what would have changed your decision.

### Checkpoint

Your account distinguishes usefulness, truth and justified reliance.

## 1. Start Here: Your First Five Minutes with AI

> Open an AI assistant and get your first useful result.

[Confident with AI course contents](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/)

Start here

Open an AI assistant and get your first useful result.

**Estimated time:** 5 minutes. **Last reviewed:** 11 August 2026.

### What you need to know

This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

Go to [www.chat.com](https://www.chat.com/) and ask your first question.

We use ChatGPT for this first exercise because it provides a simple starting point. In the next module, you can choose a different assistant.

**Learning outcome:** By the end, you will have asked an assistant for something useful and improved its first answer.

**Before you begin:** Do not enter private, confidential or identifying information during this exercise.

### The lesson

An AI assistant is a service you can talk to by typing or speaking. It generates a response based on your request.

Treat its answer as a draft or estimate, not proof.

You can ask follow-up questions: the conversation is part of the tool.

Notice that you do not need to start again. Your second instruction changes the answer within the same conversation.

### Try it

Open www.chat.com. Find the message box and ask the assistant to explain something you already understand.

If you cannot think of a subject, ask: “Explain why we have seasons.”

When it replies, say:

> Make that shorter and give me one example.

### If you get stuck

You may be asked to sign in or create an account, and the service may work differently in different places. If you cannot reach the message box, use the [General AI Assistants Tool Card](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/tool-cards/ai-assistants/) to find another way to continue.

### Checkpoint

You received an answer, asked for one change and can explain how the second response was more useful.

> Choose an accessible, affordable place to begin.

Choose an accessible, affordable place to begin.

### What you need to know

This page stands alone. No previous AI knowledge is required. You need access to an AI assistant only for the activity.

**Learning outcome:** By the end, you will have chosen one assistant to try without treating the choice as permanent.

**Before you begin:** Do not paste private, confidential or identifying information while testing. Do not pay for a subscription merely to complete this course.

### The lesson

Begin with the service that is easiest to access on your device.

Free access is enough for this course. Do not subscribe merely to complete it.

Assistant names, prices and features change, so current product comparisons belong in Tool Cards.

See the [General AI Assistants Tool Card](https://charli.info/training/confident-with-ai/tool-cards/ai-assistants/) for services you can try.

#### What to check

- Can you create an account and sign in?
- Can you find the message box and send a message?
- Can you read and navigate the response comfortably?
- Are the features you need available without payment?

### Worked example

Priya tries two assistants. Both let her send messages, but one presents long answers more cleanly with her screen reader.

She chooses that assistant for now. She has not decided it is the best assistant—only that it is the easiest place to begin.

### Try it

Use the General AI Assistants Tool Card to choose one or two services to try. Check that you can sign in if necessary, find the message box, send a message and read the response with your preferred access method. Check that the features you need are available without payment.

### Checkpoint

You can name the assistant you will use for now, confirm that basic conversation is accessible and explain why you can change later.
